'''Sir James Fraser Stoddart''', {{postnominals|country=GBR|FRS|FRSE|HonFRSC}}<ref name=frs/> (24 May 1942 – 30 December 2024) was a British-American chemist who was Chair Professor in Chemistry at the [[University of Hong Kong]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web | url=https://www.hku.hk/press/news_detail_26533.html | title=Nobel Laureate Professor Sir Fraser Stoddart joins HKU as Chair Professor of Chemistry – All News – Media – HKU | access-date=10 May 2024 | archive-date=16 September 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240916210125/https://www.hku.hk/press/news_detail_26533.html | url-status=live }}</ref> He was the Board of Trustees Professor of Chemistry and head of the Stoddart Mechanostereochemistry Group in the Department of Chemistry at [[Northwestern University]] in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.northwestern.edu/newscenter/stories/2007/08/stoddart.html|title= Nanotechnology Star Fraser Stoddart to Join Northwestern|work= NewsCenter|publisher= [[Northwestern University]]|date= 16 August 2007|access-date= 17 August 2007|archive-date= 4 July 2019|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190704142443/https://www.northwestern.edu/newscenter/stories/2007/08/stoddart.html|url-status= dead}}</ref> He worked in the area of [[supramolecular chemistry]] and [[nanotechnology]].  Stoddart developed highly efficient syntheses of [[mechanically-interlocked molecular architectures]] such as [[molecular Borromean rings]], [[catenane]]s and [[rotaxane]]s utilising [[molecular recognition]] and [[molecular self-assembly]] processes.  He demonstrated that these topologies can be employed as molecular switches.<ref>A. Coskun, M. Banaszak, [[Raymond Dean Astumian|R. D. Astumian]], J. F. Stoddart, B. A. Grzybowski, [https://dx.doi.org/10.1039/C1CS15262A ''Chem. Soc. Rev.'', 2012, 41, 19–30]</ref> His group has even applied these structures in the fabrication of nanoelectronic devices and [[nanoelectromechanical systems]] (NEMS).<ref>A. Coskun, J. M. Spruell, G. Barin, W. R. Dichtel, A. H. Flood, Y. Y. Botros, J. F. Stoddart. [https://dx.doi.org/10.1039/C2CS35053J ''Chem. Soc. Rev.'', '''2012''', ''41'' (14), 4827–59.]</ref> His efforts were recognized by numerous awards, including the 2007 [[King Faisal International Prize]] in Science.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=The ==Early life and education==
Fraser Stoddart was born in [[Edinburgh]], [[Scotland]], on 24 May 1942,<ref name=whoswho/> the only child of Tom and Jean Stoddart.<ref name="Capecelatro, Alex N. 2007">Capecelatro, Alex N. (2007). "From Auld Reekie to the City of Angels, and all the Meccano in between: A Glimpse into the Life and Mind of Sir Fraser Stoddart" (PDF). The UCLA USJ. 20. Archived from the original (PDF) on 31 March 2016. Retrieved 27 May 2016.</ref><ref name="Sir J 2018">"Sir J. Fraser Stoddart – Facts". NobelPrize.org. Retrieved 18 November 2018.</ref> He was brought up as a tenant farmer on Edgelaw Farm, a small community consisting of three families. Sir Fraser professed a passion for jigsaw puzzles and construction toys in his formative years, which he believed was the basis for his interest in molecular construction.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2016/stoddart/lecture/ | title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2016 | access-date=19 November 2018 | archive-date=19 November 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119092124/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2016/stoddart/lecture/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

Stoddart received early schooling at the local village school in [[Carrington, Midlothian]], before going on to [[Melville College]] in Edinburgh.<ref name="Capecelatro">{{cite journal|last1=Capecelatro|first1=Alex N.|title=From Auld Reekie to the City of Angels, and all the Meccano in between: A Glimpse into the Life and Mind of Sir Fraser Stoddart|journal=The UCLA USJ|date=2007|volume=20|url=http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Interviews/Interview1.pdf|access-date=27 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160331234220/http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Interviews/Interview1.pdf|archive-date=31 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name = Melville>{{cite web|url= http://issuu.com/stewartsmelvillefpnews/docs/fp_news_2014|title= It's all Kids Stuff|author= <!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|date= December 2014|website= FP News, The magazine and Annual Review of The Stewart's Melville FP Club|publisher= Daniel Stewart's and Melville College Former Pupils Club|pages= 13–14|access-date= 29 July 2015|archive-date= 21 March 2016|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160321180218/https://issuu.com/stewartsmelvillefpnews/docs/fp_news_2014|url-status= live}}</ref> He started at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1960 where he initially studied chemistry, physics and mathematics.<ref name="Capecelatro, Alex N. 2007"/> He was awarded a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in Chemistry in 1964 followed by a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1966<ref name=stodphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Edinburgh|title=Studies on plant gums of the Acacia group|first=James Fraser|last=Stoddart|date=1967|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.662504|archive-date=6 October 2016|access-date=5 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006205612/http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.662504|url-status=live}}</ref> for research on [[natural gum]]s in ''[[Acacia]]s'' supervised by Sir [[Edmund Langley Hirst]] and D M W Anderson<ref name=cv/> from the University of Edinburgh.<ref>"2005 – Professor J Fraser Stoddart". The University of Edinburgh. Retrieved 26 May 2016.</ref>

==Career==
In 1967, Stoddart went to [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] (Canada) as a [[National Research Council of Canada|National Research Council]] Postdoctoral Fellow. In 1970 he moved to the [[University of Sheffield]] as an [[Imperial Chemical Industries]] (ICI) Research Fellow, before joining the academic staff as a lecturer in chemistry. In early 1978 he was a [[Science Research Council]] Senior Visiting Fellow at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry. Later in 1978, he was transferred to the ICI Corporate Laboratory in [[Runcorn]], England where he first started investigating the mechanically interlocked molecules that would eventually become molecular machines.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2016/stoddart/lecture/|title=Sir J. Fraser Stoddart – Facts|website=NobelPrize.org|access-date=18 November 2018|archive-date=19 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119092124/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2016/stoddart/lecture/|url-status=live}}</ref> At the end of the three year secondment he returned to Sheffield<ref name="Marcus"/> where he was promoted to a Readership in 1982.

Stoddart was awarded a [[Doctor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1980<ref name=stodsc>{{cite thesis|degree=DSc|publisher=University of Edinburgh|title=Some adventures in stereochemistry|first= James Fraser|last=Stoddart|date=1980|oclc=605975820|hdl=1842/14487}} {{open access}}</ref> for his research into [[stereochemistry]] beyond the molecule. In 1990, he moved to the Chair of [[Organic Chemistry]] at the [[University of Birmingham]] and was Head of the School of Chemistry there (1993–97) before moving to UCLA as the [[Saul Winstein]] Professor of Chemistry in 1997, succeeding Nobel laureate [[Donald Cram]].<ref name="CNANOI"/><ref name="Wolpert"/>

In July 2002, Stoddart became the Acting Co-Director of the [[California NanoSystems Institute]] (CNSI). In May 2003, he became the [[Fred Kavli]] Chair of NanoSystems Sciences and served from then through August 2007 as the Director of the CNSI.<ref name="Wolpert">{{cite web|last1=Wolpert|first1=Stuart|title=UCLA Chemist Fraser Stoddart Named Director of California NanoSystems Institute|url=http://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/UCLA-Chemist-Fraser-Stoddart-Named-4695|website=UCLA Newsroom|date=6 November 2003|access-date=26 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006210223/http://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/UCLA-Chemist-Fraser-Stoddart-Named-4695|archive-date=6 October 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2008, Stoddart established the Mechanostereochemistry Group and was named Board of Trustees Professor in Chemistry at Northwestern University.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2016/10/fraser-stoddart-awarded-nobel-prize-in-chemistry/|title=Sir Fraser Stoddart is awarded Nobel Prize in Chemistry|website=news.northwestern.edu}}</ref> He went on to be the Director of the Center for the Chemistry of Integrated Systems (CCIS) at Northwestern University in 2010.<ref>"James Fraser Stoddart: Curriculum Vitae, Full Version" (PDF). stoddart.northwestern.edu. Archived from the original (PDF) on 5 October 2016.</ref>

In 2017, Stoddart was appointed a part-time position at the [[University of New South Wales]] to establish his ''New Chemistry'' initiative at the UNSW School of Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|author1=z3523783 |url=https://newsroom.unsw.edu.au/news/science-tech/unsw-appoints-2016-nobel-prize-winner-chemistry-professor-sir-fraser-stoddart|title=UNSW appoints 2016 Nobel Prize winner in Chemistry, Professor Sir Fraser Stoddart|date=15 December 2017|website=UNSW Newsroom|access-date=11 March 2019|archive-date=12 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180412192402/https://newsroom.unsw.edu.au/news/science-tech/unsw-appoints-2016-nobel-prize-winner-chemistry-professor-sir-fraser-stoddart|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2019, Stoddart introduced a skincare brand called Noble Panacea.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.vogue.com/slideshow/noble-panacea-met-event-launch | title=Skin-Care Line Noble Panacea Launched with a Glitzy, Model-Heavy Gala at the Met | date=23 October 2019 | access-date=3 November 2019 | archive-date=3 November 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191103122219/https://www.vogue.com/slideshow/noble-panacea-met-event-launch | url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2021, Stoddart co-founded a startup called H2MOF, dedicated to solving the challenges associated with hydrogen storage and transportation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our founders |url=https://h2mof.com/our-founders/ |access-date=4 July 2024 |website=H2MOF |date=8 June 2023 |language=en-US |archive-date=13 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240713191957/https://h2mof.com/our-founders/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2023, Stoddart joined the University of Hong Kong as Chair Professor of Chemistry.<ref name="auto"/>

During 35 years, nearly 300 PhD students and [[postdoctoral research]]ers have been trained in his laboratories.<ref name="Capecelatro"/>

==Research==
Stoddart is one of only a few chemists of the past quarter century to have pioneered a new field in organic chemistry.  By establishing a new field where the main feature is mechanical bonds, he paved the way for molecular recognition, self-assembly processes for template-directed mechanically interlocked syntheses, molecular switches, and motor-molecules. These advances have formed the basis of the fields of nanoelectronic devices, nanoelectromechanical systems, and molecular machines.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stoddart.northwestern.edu/fraser-stoddart/|title=Fraser Stoddart – Stoddart Mechanostereochemistry Group|website=stoddart.northwestern.edu|language=en-US|access-date=19 November 2018|archive-date=28 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190828025726/https://stoddart.northwestern.edu/fraser-stoddart/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NP-20161005" />

One of his major contributions to the development of [[mechanically-interlocked molecular architectures]] such as [[rotaxane]]s and [[catenane]]s was the establishment of efficient synthetic protocols based on the binding of [[cyclobis(paraquat-p-phenylene)|cyclobis(paraquat-''p''-phenylene)]] with electron-rich aromatic guests.<ref name="Stoddart 2009 p=1802">{{cite journal | last=Stoddart | first=J. Fraser | title=The chemistry of the mechanical bond | journal=Chemical Society Reviews | publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC) | volume=38 | issue=6 | year=2009 | pages=1802–1820 | issn=0306-0012 | doi=10.1039/b819333a | pmid=19587969 }}</ref> His group reported the synthesis of an advanced mechanically interlocked molecular architecture called [[molecular Borromean rings]] through the use of [[dynamic covalent chemistry]].<ref name="Chichak pp. 1308–1312">{{cite journal | last=Chichak | first=K. S. | title=Molecular Borromean Rings | journal=Science | publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) | volume=304 | issue=5675 | date=28 May 2004 | issn=0036-8075 | doi=10.1126/science.1096914 | pages=1308–1312 | pmid=15166376 | bibcode=2004Sci...304.1308C | s2cid=45191675 | url=http://irep.ntu.ac.uk/id/eprint/22968/1/196491_534%20Cave%20PostPrint.pdf | archive-date=24 February 2021 | access-date=8 July 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224134726/http://irep.ntu.ac.uk/id/eprint/22968/1/196491_534%20Cave%20PostPrint.pdf | url-status=live }}</ref> The efficient procedures developed to synthesize these molecular architectures was applied to the construction of [[molecular switch]]es that operate based on the movement of the various components with respect to one another.  These interlocked molecules have potential uses as [[molecular sensor]]s, [[actuators]], [[amplifiers]], and [[molecular switch]]es, and can be controlled chemically, electrically, and optically.<ref name="Science Watch">{{cite journal|title=UCLA's J. Fraser Stoddart on Switching to Molecular Electronics|journal=Science Watch|date=2005|volume=16|issue=5|url=http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Interviews/Interview3.pdf|access-date=27 May 2016|archive-date=31 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160331235024/http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Interviews/Interview3.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

{{blockquote|His work bridged the gap between chemistry and the scientific and engineering challenges of nanoelectromechanical systems."<ref name = Davy/>}}

Stoddart pioneered the use of [[mechanically interlocked molecular architectures]] to create [[Nanomechanics|nanomechanical systems]].<ref name="Richards"/><ref name="Madou">{{cite book|last1=Madou|first1=Marc J.|title=From MEMS to bio-MEMS and bio-NEMS : manufacturing techniques and applications|date=2009|publisher=CRC|location=Boca Raton, Fla.|isbn=978-1-4200-5516-0|pages=131–133|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IBzSBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA132|access-date=27 May 2016}}</ref> He has demonstrated that such devices can be fabricated using a combination of the [[Top-down and bottom-up design|bottom-up]] approach of [[molecular self-assembly]] and a [[Top-down and bottom-up design|top-down approach]] of [[lithography]] and [[microfabrication]].<ref name="Tseng">{{cite journal|last1=Stoddart|first1=J. F.|last2=Tseng|first2=H.-R.|title=Chemical synthesis gets a fillip from molecular recognition and self-assembly processes|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=12 March 2002|volume=99|issue=8|pages=4797–4800|doi=10.1073/pnas.052708999|pmc=122671|pmid=11891314|bibcode=2002PNAS...99.4797F|doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{blockquote|The credit for making molecular machines attractive to chemists goes to Fraser Stoddart, (... who) had the vision to realise that these architectures gave you the possibility of large amplitude-controlled motions, and that that could be the basis of molecular machines. <p>— [[David Leigh (scientist)|David Leigh]].<ref name="Richards">{{cite journal|last1=Richards|first1=Victoria|title=Molecular Machines|journal=Chemistry World|date=16 February 2016|url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/molecular-machines/9457.article|archive-date=31 May 2019|access-date=6 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190531140622/https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/molecular-machines/9457.article|url-status=live}}</ref></p>}}

===Presentation style===
{{external media | width = 180px | float = right | headerimage= [[File:Molecular Solomon's knot AngewChemIntEd 2007 v46 p218.jpg | 170px]] | video1 = [http://steamconnect.org/fraser-stoddart-mingling-art-with-science/ "Fraser Stoddart: Mingling Art with Science"], STE[+a]M Connect | video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=96uHJq4yqCY "The Beauty and Promise of Molecular Nanotechnology"], PSW Science | video3 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1wfeBIpYooA "Fraser Stoddart on Molecular Assembly"], 1990, [[University of Birmingham]] }}

Stoddart's papers and other material are instantly recognizable due to a distinctive "[[cartoon]]"-style of [[scientific visualization|representation]] he developed beginning in the late 1980s. A solid circle is often placed in the middle of the [[aromatic]] rings of the molecular structures he has reported, and different colours to highlight different parts of the molecules. The different colours usually correspond to the different parts of a cartoon representation of the molecule, but are also used to represent specific molecular properties (blue, for example, is used to represent [[electron acceptor|electron-poor recognition units]] while red is used to represent the corresponding [[electron donor|electron-rich recognition units]]). The distinctive colouring has led to coining the term 'little blue box' for the cyclophane cyclobis(paraquat-''p''-phenylene); an important π-acceptor used to synthesize mechanically bonded structures.<ref name=":0" /> Stoddart maintains this standardized colour scheme across all of his publications and presentations, and his style has been adopted by other researchers reporting mechanically interlocked molecules based on his syntheses.<ref name="Art">{{cite news|title=Fraser Stoddart: Mingling Art with Science|url=http://steamconnect.org/fraser-stoddart-mingling-art-with-science/|access-date=27 May 2016|work=Ste(a)m Connect|archive-date=23 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160623211417/http://steamconnect.org/fraser-stoddart-mingling-art-with-science/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Brough">{{cite journal|last1=Brough|first1=B.|last2=Northrop|first2=B. H.|last3=Schmidt|first3=J. J.|last4=Tseng|first4=H.-R.|last5=Houk|first5=K. N.|last6=Stoddart|first6=J. F.|last7=Ho|first7=C.-M.|title=Evaluation of synthetic linear motor-molecule actuation energetics|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=30 May 2006|volume=103|issue=23|pages=8583–8588|doi=10.1073/pnas.0509645103|pmc=1482623|pmid=16735470|bibcode=2006PNAS..103.8583B|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Fraser Stoddart: Chemistry H-index & Awards | website=Research.com | url=https://research.com/u/j-fraser-stoddart | access-date=3 January 2025 | archive-date=3 February 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230203232938/https://research.com/u/j-fraser-stoddart | url-status=live }}</ref> As of 2023 he had published more than 1200 publications.<ref name="Publications">{{cite web | title=Publications – Stoddart Mechanostereochemistry Group | website=Stoddart Mechanostereochemistry Group – Chemistry & Molecular Nanotechnology in Tomorrow's World | date=12 August 2023 | url=https://stoddart.northwestern.edu/publications/ | access-date=3 January 2025 | archive-date=15 September 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240915073600/https://stoddart.northwestern.edu/publications/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Stoddart was an American and British citizen. He was married to Norma Agnes Scholan from 1968<ref name=whoswho/><ref name="Award"/><ref name="Scotsman"/> until her death in 2004 from cancer.<ref name=":0" /> They had two daughters: Fiona Jane and Alison Margaret.<ref name=whoswho/> Norma Stoddart obtained a PhD in biochemistry and helped support the research efforts of her husband at the Universities of Sheffield, Birmingham, and California, Los Angeles.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/latimes/obituary.aspx?n=norma-agnes-stoddart&pid=1799050|title=Obituary – Norma Agnes Stoddart|date=14 January 2004|website=Los Angeles Times|access-date=18 November 2018|archive-date=19 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119132912/https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/latimes/obituary.aspx?n=norma-agnes-stoddart&pid=1799050|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 30 December 2024, Stoddart died from [[cardiac arrest]] at a hotel in Melbourne, Australia, where he was visiting his daughter, at the age of 82.<ref>{{cite web|title=J. Fraser Stoddart, Who Developed Microscopic Machines, Dies at 82|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/11/science/j-fraser-stoddart-dead.html|date=11 January 2025|last=McClain|first=Dylan Loeb|work=The New York Times|access-date=11 January 2025}}</ref><ref name="h186">{{cite web | last=Yiu | first=William | title=Fraser Stoddart, Nobel laureate and professor at University of Hong Kong, dies | website=South China Morning Post | date=31 December 2024 | url=https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/education/article/3292928/fraser-stoddart-nobel-laureate-and-professor-university-hong-kong-dies | ==Philanthropy==
The Fraser and Norma Stoddart Prize for PhD students was established at their alma mater, the University of Edinburgh.<ref name="Award">{{cite web|title=Alumnus Presents New Prize for PhD Students|url=http://www.chem.ed.ac.uk/alumni/get-informed/newsletter-issue-5/alumnus-presents-new-prize-phd-students|access-date=27 May 2016|website=University of Edinburgh|archive-date=1 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701065749/http://www.chem.ed.ac.uk/alumni/get-informed/newsletter-issue-5/alumnus-presents-new-prize-phd-students|url-status=dead}}</ref> It was first awarded in 2013.<ref name="Prize">{{cite web|title=First Ever Fraser and Norma Stoddart Prize|url=http://www.ecampbell.chem.ed.ac.uk/news/first-ever-fraser-and-norma-stoddart-prize|website=University of Edinburgh|access-date=24 May 2013|archive-date=1 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701061240/http://www.ecampbell.chem.ed.ac.uk/news/first-ever-fraser-and-norma-stoddart-prize|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Stoddart was appointed a [[Knight Bachelor]] in the New Year's Honours December 2006, by [[Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom|Queen Elizabeth II]] for Services to Chemistry and Molecular Nanotechnology.<ref name="Marcus">{{cite web|last1=Marcus|first1=Jennifer|title=UCLA's J. Fraser Stoddart Adds Knight Bachelor to His List of Honors|url=http://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/UCLA-s-J-Fraser-Stoddart-Adds-7598|website=UCLA Newsroom|date=4 January 2007|access-date=27 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190218202130/http://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/UCLA-s-J-Fraser-Stoddart-Adds-7598|archive-date=18 February 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Knight>{{cite web|url= http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Index.php?View=News/NewsSheet.php&ID=77|title= Ma'am to the Rescue|access-date= 19 January 2009|publisher= Stoddart Mechanostereochemistry Group|date= 13 June 2007|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100612192443/http://stoddart.northwestern.edu/Index.php?View=News%2FNewsSheet.php&ID=77|archive-date= 12 June 2010|url-status= dead}}</ref>

In 2007, he received the [[Albert Einstein World Award of Science]] in recognition for his outstanding and pioneering work in molecular recognition and self-assembly, and the introduction of quick and efficient template-directed synthetic routes to mechanically interlocked molecular compounds, which have changed the way chemists think about molecular switches and machines.<ref name="WCC">{{cite web|title=Prof. Sir Fraser Stoddart|url=http://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/winners/winners-of-the-world-award-of-science/prof-sir-fraser-stoddart/|website=World Cultural Council|date=24 November 2007|access-date=6 October 2016|archive-date=10 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161010172245/http://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/winners/winners-of-the-world-award-of-science/prof-sir-fraser-stoddart/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2016, he shared the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] together with [[Ben Feringa]] and [[Jean-Pierre Sauvage]] for the design and synthesis of [[molecular machine]]s.<ref name="NP-20161005"/><ref name=":1" />
